core.text: When a sentence reports an order, a request or a wish, the thing wanted goes into a clause with **ut / ne + subjunctive (the form for what someone asks or orders someone to do)**: *imperat ut mercēdem solvat* — he orders him to pay the rent; *ōrat nē sē verberet* — he begs him not to beat him. Latin name: *coniunctivus substantivus: ut, ne*.
English uses *to*: *he told the farmer to pay*, *she asked her not to leave*. The *to*-phrase is the command.
Verb of ordering, asking, warning or wishing + ut (nē for 'not') + subjunctive. Lead-ins: imperō, rogō, ōrō, moneō, postulō, cūrō, hortor, volō.

invented.la: Māter fīliō imperat nē in viā lūdat.
invented.en: The mother orders her son not to play in the street.

core.text: After a verb of doing the same *ut* + subjunctive is **ut / ne + subjunctive (the 'in order to' clause: venit ut videat = comes to see)** — it says why. After *imperat, rogat, monet* it says what was ordered. Ask: is *ut* completing a verb of telling, or explaining an action?

more.text: The learner's notes (week 27) call this the substantive subjunctive: a noun clause for a wish, command or tendency rather than a fact. Their examples: *dux imperat ut mīlitēs sequantur*; *volō ut omnēs veniāmus*; *mōs est Rōmānīs ut ad cēnam discumbant*; and *accidit ut …* / *fit ut …* (it happens that …).

The clause verb is present subjunctive after a present main verb and imperfect after a past one (*rogāvit ut nārrāret*); that pairing is the sequence of tenses. Two verbs of ordering skip *ut*: *iubeō* and *vetō* take the accusative + infinitive (*iubet eum venīre*). Verbs of saying and thinking never take *ut*; they take the accusative + infinitive (*dīcit eum venīre*). A second negative in the clause is *nēve*: *cūrā nē ovēs aberrent nēve silvam petant*.
